Dependencies and the project schedule

Unit 1 · Week 8 · Lesson 2 · Suggested 55-minute plan; adjust to local timing.

Prepare: Use the agreed R1 to R5 brief, project workbook section 2, and a blank ten-lesson timeline. Paper or an approved spreadsheet is suitable.

Suggested answers are teacher guidance, not extra assessment tasks. These notes are public.

1. Dependencies and the project schedule

Suggested time: 2 minutes

Instructional strategy: Learning intention

Success means sequence tasks using real dependencies, sketch a Gantt chart for the ten project lessons, and reserve time for corrections and user acceptance. The sample schedule is a proposal students may justify and revise.

2. Retrieval: a task needs a reason

Suggested time: 5 minutes

Instructional strategy: Individual retrieval and think-pair-share

Expected R4 concerns retained records over two runs, R5 includes ties and empty sessions. A measurable check compares an actual result to a predetermined expectation. Ask which requirement informs the record format. Link last lesson’s decisions to practical tasks in the schedule.

3. Dependencies determine the order

Suggested time: 6 minutes

Instructional strategy: Card sort and justification

Give pairs task labels: agree record format, implement append, calculate cost, test cost, integrate modules, trial with organiser. Record format precedes append implementation. Calculation implementation precedes an execution test, though expected results can be designed now. Integration depends on compatible interfaces and tested components. Permit overlapping planning and testing when justified.

4. Ten project lessons

Suggested time: 10 minutes

Instructional strategy: Worked timeline and calendar check

The chapter allocates four project lessons in week 8, two in week 9 and four in week 10. Week 9 lessons 1 and 2 teach APIs/attribution and debugging, so do not count them as extra project workshops. P1 to P10 are local planning labels, not official lesson numbers. Today is P2. Have students label each timeline slot with its actual week and lesson.

5. A Gantt chart proposal

Suggested time: 10 minutes

Instructional strategy: Teacher modelling and paired critique

Each filled dot marks a planned task period. Ranges refer to project slots shown on the previous slide. In P1 to P4, plan and desk-check tests rather than claim executed code results. Build in P5 to P7 includes unit and integration tests. P8 reserves whole-system tests and corrections, P9 the organiser trial and P10 demonstration/evaluation. Students redraw at ten individual slot resolution and refine. This is one feasible plan, not proof every task will finish on time.

6. Your schedule and milestones

Suggested time: 12 minutes

Instructional strategy: Paired planning with independent records

Students complete workbook section 2 and draw a ten-slot Gantt chart. Include requirements, interfaces/data, implementation, tests/corrections, acceptance and evaluation. Record dependencies and evidence for design review at end of week 8, build review at end of week 9 and final demonstration in week 10. Distinguish planned and actual completion. Support: supply task names. Extension: justify which tasks can overlap without creating conflicting interfaces.

7. A delay needs a revised plan

Suggested time: 5 minutes

Instructional strategy: Scenario discussion and all-student response

Scenario: file storage does not pass its tests by the build review. A justified response identifies affected integration/persistence tasks, records the reason, adjusts remaining work and preserves essential testing and acceptance evidence. Avoid inventing completed dates or deleting requirements silently. Students propose a concrete change within available lessons and seek teacher feedback if scope is no longer feasible.

8. Checkpoint: a feasible schedule

Suggested time: 5 minutes

Instructional strategy: Independent exit ticket

Ask each student to show a dependency with an explanation and locate time for correction/retest. Check ten project slots rather than twelve. Retain the Gantt chart and workbook schedule, with actual progress left honest. Use plans to identify unrealistic workloads before module design.
